chunks: Why avoid radiated EMI. The question: Why do I want to avoid radiated EMI?
Radiated EMI is noise that leaves your board as radio waves. You avoid it for four reasons. The law limits it, and a product that fails cannot be sold.
It disturbs other equipment, including your own radios. A board that radiates well also picks up noise well. And fixing it late is costly, while good layout is nearly free.
Imagine an apartment with thin walls. Your loud music gets out, and the neighbor's music gets in. Whatever lets sound leak out also lets it leak in.
That is reciprocity: a structure that sends well also receives well. The building rules are the regulators' limits, and your own ear is your own radio.
Each curve rises at 40 decibels/decade (because E proportional to f squared ) and sits 9. 5 decibels higher per tripling of area, 20 decibels higher per tenfold.
The 10 cm² loop crosses the limit near 48 megahertz, the 3 cm² loop near 87 megahertz and the 1 cm² loop only near 185 megahertz.
The limit line is stepped because the standard is. (Assumes the same 10 milliamps of harmonic current at each frequency, which is a simplification.)
Emission limit: the legal ceiling on how strong a field a product may radiate, measured at a set distance. FCC and CISPR publish these.
Common-mode current: current flowing the same direction on both wires of a cable, which makes the cable an antenna.
Loop area: the area enclosed by a current's outbound and return paths. A bigger loop radiates more. Reciprocity: a structure that radiates well also receives well.
Decibel (dB): a way to compare sizes. Every 20 decibels is a factor of 10 in field strength. Desense: noise lowering a receiver's sensitivity, so it hears weak signals worse.
Take 10 milliamps of current at 100 megahertz in a loop, measured 3 m away. A 1 cm² loop is about 11 decibels under the US limit for home products (FCC Class B), so it passes.
Make the loop 10 cm². Ten times the area gives a field 10 times stronger, and now it is about 9 decibels over, so it fails.
A 30 cm cable carrying only about 12 microamps of common-mode current at 100 megahertz also reaches the limit.
That is the whole idea: tiny currents in the wrong geometry fail tests.
"Mainly four reasons. It's regulated: you can't sell a product that fails FCC or CISPR limits.
It interferes with other radios, including your own, because noise in the Wi-Fi or GPS band desensitises your receiver.
By reciprocity, anything that radiates well also picks up interference well.
And it's a symptom of bad layout: big loops and cable common-mode current also cause ringing and crosstalk.
It's very sensitive too: about 12 microamps of common-mode current on a 30 centimetre cable can reach the limit at 100 megahertz."
